transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I’m here because… well, I suppose because I got frightened by my own thoughts. Some mornings, when I wake up, or even before I’m fully out of bed, I find myself thinking it might be easier if I just hadn’t woken up at all. Not that I have a plan to do anything to myself—I don’t—but the thought is there, and it’s been unsettling enough that I felt I shouldn’t just keep brushing it aside.

I almost didn’t make the appointment because part of me kept saying, “Oh, you’re just being dramatic,” or “Everyone has low days,” but it’s the fact that it keeps coming back in the mornings that worries me. I don’t want to hurt myself, but I also don’t feel right pretending those thoughts aren’t happening. So… that’s what brought me in.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?

I’m… not completely sure how to answer “most days,” if I’m honest. I know that sounds evasive, but I don’t mean it that way. I’ve certainly had mornings where I wake up with this heavy, low feeling, and then I spend part of the day sort of moving through things without much brightness in me.

But whether it’s truly most days, I haven’t been keeping track in any careful way. Some days I can still function and seem fairly normal from the outside, so I start questioning whether I’m really “depressed” or just having a rough patch. I suppose I’d say I’ve been feeling down more often than I’d like, but I’m not sure I can confidently say exactly how many days.
How long have you been feeling this way?

About a month, I think. It started after my sister died—very suddenly, unexpectedly—and since then I haven’t really felt like I’ve gotten my footing back.

I keep trying to tell myself that of course I’m upset, anyone would be, but it’s been about four weeks now and the heaviness has sort of stayed with me. I don’t mean every single minute of every day, but since her death, that’s when I started noticing this change in myself.
Have you been worrying excessively about a lot of different things?

I’m not sure I’d call it “a lot of different things,” no. I mean, I do worry, but I don’t know that it’s this broad, constant worrying about everything, if that’s what you mean.

Lately my thoughts tend to circle around certain things, and then I second-guess myself about whether that counts as excessive or whether it’s just… understandable. I wouldn’t say I’m lying awake making lists of every possible disaster, but I also don’t feel especially settled. It’s a little hard for me to separate worry from just feeling unsettled and sad, if that makes sense.

So I suppose my answer is: not really a wide range of worries, at least not that I’ve noticed. But I may need you to clarify what you mean by excessive.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yes… I think I have. I’m still doing some of the things I normally do, so from the outside it may not look like I’ve stopped enjoying life exactly. I still make myself go to book club, for example, and I’ve gone to the dance night a couple of times because I don’t want to disappear or have people worry about me.

But when I’m there, it’s like I’m not fully in the room. I’m sitting there while everyone is talking or laughing, and I feel sort of behind a pane of glass, if that makes sense. I can see that these are the things I used to enjoy, and I know how I’m supposed to feel, but I don’t really get that same pleasure from them.

Even smaller things at home… my garden used to give me such a lift, just checking on what was coming up or fussing over the plants. And I used to really enjoy cooking something for the neighbors, especially if I had extra soup or a casserole. Lately I can still do those things, but they feel flatter. They don’t give me that little bit of warmth or satisfaction the way they used to. So yes, I suppose the interest is still there in a dutiful way, but the pleasure part has been missing.
When you feel at your lowest, are your thoughts mainly about missing your sister and her death?

I’m not entirely sure how to separate it out, honestly. A lot of the lowest moments do seem to have her in them, or at least her death is sort of the doorway into them, if that makes sense. I’ll think about something ordinary and then suddenly remember she isn’t here, and that can pull me down very quickly.

But I don’t know that I can say my thoughts are mainly only about missing her. Sometimes it feels more like this heavy feeling settles over everything, and then I may not even be thinking one clear thought. It’s more like… I’m just low, and if I try to trace it back, yes, her being gone is there. But it isn’t always a specific memory or a specific thought like “I miss my sister” running through my mind.

So I guess I’d say her death is very tied up in it, but when I’m at my lowest, it can feel broader and harder to name than just missing her.
Since this started, have there still been moments when something can genuinely lift your mood, even briefly?

Not very often, no. I mean, there are moments where I can tell something should lift my mood, if that makes sense. Like I’ll still make myself go to book club, or I’ll go to the dance night because I know it’s better than just staying home and withdrawing completely. And sometimes people are kind, or someone says something funny, and I can sort of recognize it as pleasant.

But it doesn’t really reach me the way it used to. I end up sitting there feeling a bit like I’m behind a pane of glass, watching everyone else be part of it. I’m present, but I’m not really… warmed by it, I suppose.

Even with things that used to reliably give me a little lift, like being out in my garden or cooking something for the neighbors, it’s flatter now. I still do them sometimes, but that little spark of pleasure or satisfaction just doesn’t come the same way. So if my mood lifts, it’s brief and kind of faint, not the genuine lift I remember.
Do you feel this low even when you are not thinking about your sister?

I’m not completely sure. I wish I could give you a cleaner answer, but it’s hard for me to untangle it in the moment.

There are times when I’m low and I don’t think I’m consciously thinking, “This is about my sister,” or picturing her exactly. It can just feel like the day has gone dim somehow, and I’m moving through it with that heaviness there. But then if I stop and examine it, I wonder if she’s still underneath it in some way, even if I wasn’t actively thinking about her.

So… yes, I think I can feel low even when she isn’t right at the front of my mind. But I also don’t know how much she’s still in the background, if that makes sense. It’s not always a clear thought about her, but it may still be connected.
Did these feelings begin only after your sister died?

Yes… yes, really only after she died. It’s been about a month now, maybe just a little over or under depending on how I count it, but that’s when all of this started in this way.

I mean, I’ve had sad periods in life before, of course—at my age you don’t get through everything untouched—but this particular heaviness, the way it’s been sitting on me day after day, began after my sister died unexpectedly. It felt like one day life was difficult but still recognizable, and then after that call, or after realizing she was really gone, everything shifted. Since then it’s just been… about a month of feeling like this.
Since this began, have there been any moments when you truly felt better for a while, even if only briefly?

Only in a very muted sort of way. I still make myself go to things, like book club or the dance night, because part of me knows those are the things that used to help me feel more like myself. And I don’t want to just disappear into the house and stop doing everything.

But when I’m there, it’s not the same. I can be sitting with people I like, hearing the conversation, maybe even knowing something is funny or pleasant, but it feels like it doesn’t quite get through to me. Almost like I’m behind a pane of glass, watching it happen rather than really being in it.

And that’s true at home too. My garden used to give me such a little lift, even just checking on things or pulling a few weeds, and cooking for the neighbors used to make me feel useful and warm inside. Lately I still do those things sometimes, but the feeling I used to get from them just… doesn’t arrive. So I suppose there are small moments where I’m distracted or a bit steadier, but truly better? Not really, not in the way I remember.
Before your sister died, had you ever had another period in your life when you felt depressed like this for two weeks or longer?

I don’t know that I can point to one, no—not like this, and not clearly for two weeks or longer.

I mean, I’ve had hard stretches. There were times when I felt discouraged or worn down, or when life felt lonely or disappointing for a while. I don’t want to make it sound like I’ve never been sad before, because that wouldn’t be true. But when you ask “depressed like this,” I have trouble saying yes, because this feels different in its weight and how it’s stayed with me.

So… as best as I can answer, no, I don’t think I’ve had another period before this where I felt this way for two weeks or more. Not that I can remember.
Over the past month, have you felt down or had little pleasure in things nearly every day?

Yes… nearly every day, I think. It’s not always the same intensity every hour, but it’s been there most days in one form or another.

I still make myself show up for things, like book club or the dance night, because I don’t want to just stop living my life completely, and those things used to mean something to me. But lately I’ll be sitting there, with people talking around me, and I feel like I’m behind a pane of glass. I can see that I’m supposed to be enjoying it, or I remember that I used to enjoy it, but it doesn’t really reach me.

And it’s the same with the smaller things at home. My garden used to give me this little lift, even just looking at what was coming up or fussing with the plants. Cooking for the neighbors used to make me feel useful and connected. Now I still do some of it, but the pleasure just isn’t there the way it was. So yes, I’d say it’s been nearly every day.
Over the past month, have you noticed a change in your sleep?

Yes, I have. Sleep has gotten… broken, I guess is the best way to put it.

I don’t usually have one solid stretch of sleep anymore. I’ll fall asleep for a little while, then come up again, then drift off again, almost in bits and pieces. And then very early, before it’s really morning—before dawn a lot of the time—I wake up and my mind is already going. Not necessarily in an organized way, just turning things over, and once that starts I usually can’t settle back down.

I’ll lie there trying to be still, telling myself there’s no point getting up yet, but the day has sort of already begun in my head. By the time it’s actually morning, I feel like I never really got properly rested.
When you wake up feeling at your lowest, is your first thought usually about your sister being gone?

I’m not sure I can say it’s usually that clear.

Sometimes, yes, my sister is there in my mind right away—or not even a thought exactly, more like I wake up and there’s this awareness that she’s still gone, if that makes sense. Like I haven’t had time to think anything yet, but the fact of it is already sitting there.

But other mornings it’s more vague than that. I wake up low, and it takes me a little while to know what I’m even feeling or why. It’s not always a sentence in my head like, “My sister is gone.” Sometimes it’s just heaviness first, and then the thoughts come in afterward.

So I wouldn’t want to say yes, that’s always or usually my first thought. It can be part of it, but I don’t know that I’ve tracked it closely enough to answer more definitely.
Over the past month, have you been feeling worthless or excessively guilty?

Yes… I think guilt more than worthless, though sometimes the guilt kind of turns into feeling like I failed her somehow.

I keep going back over those last weeks with my sister, almost like I’m reviewing a tape in my head. I’ll think, why didn’t I call that day, or why didn’t I stay on the phone longer, or why didn’t I ask better questions? I tell myself I should have listened more carefully, or said something more comforting, or found some more useful way to help her instead of just doing whatever I did at the time.

And part of me knows—at least rationally—that I probably couldn’t have changed what happened. I do know that. If someone else said these things to me, I’d probably tell them they were being too hard on themselves. But when it’s me, it doesn’t seem to land the same way. I keep thinking there must have been something I missed, something I should have done differently.

So yes, I’ve been feeling guilty. Excessively, maybe… I don’t know. It feels excessive when I say it out loud, but it still feels very real when I’m in it.
When you feel guilty, is it mostly about your sister and what happened around her death?

Yes, mostly. I mean, that’s where my mind goes with it almost every time.

It’s those last weeks with my sister that I keep replaying. I’ll be doing something ordinary, or lying awake, and suddenly I’m back there thinking, I should have called her more. Or I should have stayed on the phone longer when I did call. I should have listened better, picked up on something, asked the right question, done something actually useful instead of just… whatever I thought was enough at the time.

And I do understand, at least in one part of my mind, that I probably couldn’t have changed what happened. I can say that out loud. But it doesn’t stop the other part from going over it again and again, like if I review it carefully enough I’ll find the moment where I failed her. So yes, it’s mostly tied to her, and to what happened around her death.
When something genuinely good happens, does your mood lift at all in that moment?

Sometimes it does, a little, but not the way it used to. That’s the part that’s been unsettling, honestly.

I still make myself go to things. Like I’ll go to book club, or I’ll go to the dance night if I said I would, because I know if I stop going entirely that probably isn’t good for me. And sometimes something nice is happening right in front of me—someone says something funny, or everyone’s talking about a book, or the music is on—and I can recognize, intellectually, that this is pleasant. I can even smile or laugh in the right place.

But inside it’s… muted. Like I’m there, but I’m behind a pane of glass watching it instead of really being in it. The good thing happens, and I see that it’s good, but it doesn’t quite reach me.

Even things that used to give me that small lift—my garden, especially, or cooking something for the neighbors—lately I still do them, but the little spark I used to get from them isn’t really there. I might be glad I did it afterward in a kind of dutiful way, but it doesn’t brighten me the way it used to. So yes, maybe there’s a slight lift sometimes, but it feels very brief and far away.
Have you been feeling worthless?

Not worthless exactly… not all the time, anyway. It’s more that I feel like I failed her, and that can start to feel like something is wrong with me.

I keep going back over those last weeks with my sister and picking apart every little thing I did or didn’t do. I’ll think, why didn’t I call more often, why didn’t I stay on the phone longer, why didn’t I listen better? Maybe if I’d asked a different question, or noticed something in her voice, or done something more useful, then… I don’t know. I know I can’t really prove any of that, and part of me does understand I probably couldn’t have changed what happened.

But I still keep putting it on myself. So I don’t walk around thinking, “I’m worthless” in those exact words, but I do get into this place where I feel like I wasn’t enough for her when it mattered.
Have you been feeling hopeless?

Hopeless… I’m not completely sure how to answer that.

I don’t think I walk around thinking, “There is no hope,” in a clear way like that. It’s more that sometimes everything feels very heavy and hard to imagine changing. But I don’t know if that’s hopelessness exactly, or just being worn down and sad and stuck in the same thoughts.

There are moments when I can still picture things being a little easier someday, or at least I tell myself they might be. So I wouldn’t say I feel hopeless all the time. It’s just… I don’t feel very confident right now either, if that makes sense.
When you feel low, does it usually come on after something reminds you of your sister?

I’m not sure it’s that neat, honestly. Sometimes, yes, I’ll notice I’m thinking about her and then my mood sinks, but other times I’m already low and then I realize I’ve been sort of circling around thoughts of her in the background.

It isn’t always a clear trigger, like seeing a photograph or hearing a song or something. I wish it were that simple, because then I could at least point to it and say, “That’s what set me off.” A lot of the time it feels more gradual than that, like the sadness is just there and then attaches itself to whatever reminds me of her.

So… I guess I haven’t noticed a reliable pattern. It can be connected, but I don’t know that it usually comes on only after a reminder.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when the feelings began in relation to the sister's death, which is directly about onset and duration.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, really only after she died. It’s been about a month now, maybe just a little over or under depending on how I count it, but that’s when all of this started in this way.

I mean, I’ve had sad periods in life before, of course—at my age you don’t get through everything untouched—but this particular heaviness, the way it’s been sitting on me day after day, began after my sister died unexpectedly. It felt like one day life was difficult but still recognizable, and then after that call, or after realizing she was really gone, everything shifted. Since then it’s just been… about a month of feeling like this.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the low mood is mood-reactive, to distinguish an adjustment disorder related to bereavement from a major depressive episode or persistent depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Since this began, have there been any moments when you truly felt better for a while, even if only briefly?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I still make myself show up for things like book club or the dance night, but lately I sit there feeling like I'm behind a pane of glass, and even my garden and cooking for the neighbors don't give me that little lift they used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether anything can genuinely lift the patient's mood or bring pleasure, which directly relates to diminished interest or pleasure in activities.

patient.answer:
Only in a very muted sort of way. I still make myself go to things, like book club or the dance night, because part of me knows those are the things that used to help me feel more like myself. And I don’t want to just disappear into the house and stop doing everything.

But when I’m there, it’s not the same. I can be sitting with people I like, hearing the conversation, maybe even knowing something is funny or pleasant, but it feels like it doesn’t quite get through to me. Almost like I’m behind a pane of glass, watching it happen rather than really being in it.

And that’s true at home too. My garden used to give me such a little lift, even just checking on things or pulling a few weeds, and cooking for the neighbors used to make me feel useful and warm inside. Lately I still do those things sometimes, but the feeling I used to get from them just… doesn’t arrive. So I suppose there are small moments where I’m distracted or a bit steadier, but truly better? Not really, not in the way I remember.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this is an isolated episode versus part of prior depressive episodes, to distinguish adjustment disorder from major depressive disorder and single-episode from recurrent depression.
doctor.question: Before your sister died, had you ever had another period in your life when you felt depressed like this for two weeks or longer?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about past episodes of depression before the current one, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I can point to one, no—not like this, and not clearly for two weeks or longer.

I mean, I’ve had hard stretches. There were times when I felt discouraged or worn down, or when life felt lonely or disappointing for a while. I don’t want to make it sound like I’ve never been sad before, because that wouldn’t be true. But when you ask “depressed like this,” I have trouble saying yes, because this feels different in its weight and how it’s stayed with me.

So… as best as I can answer, no, I don’t think I’ve had another period before this where I felt this way for two weeks or more. Not that I can remember.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are occurring nearly every day, which helps distinguish a major depressive episode from an adjustment disorder after bereavement.
doctor.question: Over the past month, have you felt down or had little pleasure in things nearly every day?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I still make myself show up for things like book club or the dance night, but lately I sit there feeling like I'm behind a pane of glass, and even my garden and cooking for the neighbors don't give me that little lift they used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about little pleasure in things over the past month, which directly corresponds to loss of interest or diminished pleasure.

patient.answer:
Yes… nearly every day, I think. It’s not always the same intensity every hour, but it’s been there most days in one form or another.

I still make myself show up for things, like book club or the dance night, because I don’t want to just stop living my life completely, and those things used to mean something to me. But lately I’ll be sitting there, with people talking around me, and I feel like I’m behind a pane of glass. I can see that I’m supposed to be enjoying it, or I remember that I used to enjoy it, but it doesn’t really reach me.

And it’s the same with the smaller things at home. My garden used to give me this little lift, even just looking at what was coming up or fussing with the plants. Cooking for the neighbors used to make me feel useful and connected. Now I still do some of it, but the pleasure just isn’t there the way it was. So yes, I’d say it’s been nearly every day.

inference.note: Sx began only after sister’s death but now meet a depressive syndrome pattern nearly every day for ~1 month with persistent low mood/anhedonia and passive death wishes; this makes a single depressive episode more likely and rules against recurrent depression and dysthymia.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a major depressive episode from an adjustment reaction by assessing a core biological depressive symptom that supports MDD when present independently of grief.
doctor.question: Over the past month, have you noticed a change in your sleep?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: I fall asleep in bits and pieces, then wake up before dawn with my mind already turning, and I usually can't get settled again before the day starts.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about changes in sleep over the past month.

patient.answer:
Yes, I have. Sleep has gotten… broken, I guess is the best way to put it.

I don’t usually have one solid stretch of sleep anymore. I’ll fall asleep for a little while, then come up again, then drift off again, almost in bits and pieces. And then very early, before it’s really morning—before dawn a lot of the time—I wake up and my mind is already going. Not necessarily in an organized way, just turning things over, and once that starts I usually can’t settle back down.

I’ll lie there trying to be still, telling myself there’s no point getting up yet, but the day has sort of already begun in my head. By the time it’s actually morning, I feel like I never really got properly rested.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's low mood is specifically tied to grief-related thoughts versus pervasive and not limited to the loss, to distinguish adjustment disorder from a major depressive episode.
doctor.question: When you wake up feeling at your lowest, is your first thought usually about your sister being gone?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether the low mood on waking is specifically focused on thoughts of the sister being gone, which is a grief-related thought content not directly covered by the listed symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can say it’s usually that clear.

Sometimes, yes, my sister is there in my mind right away—or not even a thought exactly, more like I wake up and there’s this awareness that she’s still gone, if that makes sense. Like I haven’t had time to think anything yet, but the fact of it is already sitting there.

But other mornings it’s more vague than that. I wake up low, and it takes me a little while to know what I’m even feeling or why. It’s not always a sentence in my head like, “My sister is gone.” Sometimes it’s just heaviness first, and then the thoughts come in afterward.

So I wouldn’t want to say yes, that’s always or usually my first thought. It can be part of it, but I don’t know that I’ve tracked it closely enough to answer more definitely.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has excessive guilt or feelings of worthlessness, which would favor a major depressive episode over an adjustment disorder/grief reaction.
doctor.question: Over the past month, have you been feeling worthless or excessively guilty?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep going over the last weeks with my sister and telling myself I should have called more, listened better, done something more useful, even when part of me knows I couldn't have changed what happened.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about feeling worthless or excessively guilty over the past month.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think guilt more than worthless, though sometimes the guilt kind of turns into feeling like I failed her somehow.

I keep going back over those last weeks with my sister, almost like I’m reviewing a tape in my head. I’ll think, why didn’t I call that day, or why didn’t I stay on the phone longer, or why didn’t I ask better questions? I tell myself I should have listened more carefully, or said something more comforting, or found some more useful way to help her instead of just doing whatever I did at the time.

And part of me knows—at least rationally—that I probably couldn’t have changed what happened. I do know that. If someone else said these things to me, I’d probably tell them they were being too hard on themselves. But when it’s me, it doesn’t seem to land the same way. I keep thinking there must have been something I missed, something I should have done differently.

So yes, I’ve been feeling guilty. Excessively, maybe… I don’t know. It feels excessive when I say it out loud, but it still feels very real when I’m in it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the guilt is specifically tied to the loss or instead generalized/self-critical beyond bereavement, to distinguish adjustment disorder from a major depressive episode.
doctor.question: When you feel guilty, is it mostly about your sister and what happened around her death?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep going over the last weeks with my sister and telling myself I should have called more, listened better, done something more useful, even when part of me knows I couldn't have changed what happened.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about the content and focus of the patient's guilty feelings, which directly corresponds to the Worthlessness_Guilt symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yes, mostly. I mean, that’s where my mind goes with it almost every time.

It’s those last weeks with my sister that I keep replaying. I’ll be doing something ordinary, or lying awake, and suddenly I’m back there thinking, I should have called her more. Or I should have stayed on the phone longer when I did call. I should have listened better, picked up on something, asked the right question, done something actually useful instead of just… whatever I thought was enough at the time.

And I do understand, at least in one part of my mind, that I probably couldn’t have changed what happened. I can say that out loud. But it doesn’t stop the other part from going over it again and again, like if I review it carefully enough I’ll find the moment where I failed her. So yes, it’s mostly tied to her, and to what happened around her death.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's low mood is mood-reactive to positive events, which helps distinguish major depressive episode from an adjustment disorder/grief-related reaction.
doctor.question: When something genuinely good happens, does your mood lift at all in that moment?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I still make myself show up for things like book club or the dance night, but lately I sit there feeling like I'm behind a pane of glass, and even my garden and cooking for the neighbors don't give me that little lift they used to.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether positive events still produce any emotional lift or pleasure, which most directly relates to diminished interest or pleasure.

patient.answer:
Sometimes it does, a little, but not the way it used to. That’s the part that’s been unsettling, honestly.

I still make myself go to things. Like I’ll go to book club, or I’ll go to the dance night if I said I would, because I know if I stop going entirely that probably isn’t good for me. And sometimes something nice is happening right in front of me—someone says something funny, or everyone’s talking about a book, or the music is on—and I can recognize, intellectually, that this is pleasant. I can even smile or laugh in the right place.

But inside it’s… muted. Like I’m there, but I’m behind a pane of glass watching it instead of really being in it. The good thing happens, and I see that it’s good, but it doesn’t quite reach me.

Even things that used to give me that small lift—my garden, especially, or cooking something for the neighbors—lately I still do them, but the little spark I used to get from them isn’t really there. I might be glad I did it afterward in a kind of dutiful way, but it doesn’t brighten me the way it used to. So yes, maybe there’s a slight lift sometimes, but it feels very brief and far away.

doctor.intent: Differentiate major depressive episode from adjustment disorder by testing whether there is a distinct depressive cognitive symptom not limited to grief-related guilt.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling worthless?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep going over the last weeks with my sister and telling myself I should have called more, listened better, done something more useful, even when part of me knows I couldn't have changed what happened.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about feeling worthless, which is covered by the worthlessness/guilt symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Not worthless exactly… not all the time, anyway. It’s more that I feel like I failed her, and that can start to feel like something is wrong with me.

I keep going back over those last weeks with my sister and picking apart every little thing I did or didn’t do. I’ll think, why didn’t I call more often, why didn’t I stay on the phone longer, why didn’t I listen better? Maybe if I’d asked a different question, or noticed something in her voice, or done something more useful, then… I don’t know. I know I can’t really prove any of that, and part of me does understand I probably couldn’t have changed what happened.

But I still keep putting it on myself. So I don’t walk around thinking, “I’m worthless” in those exact words, but I do get into this place where I feel like I wasn’t enough for her when it mattered.

doctor.intent: Differentiate major depressive episode from adjustment disorder by determining whether the patient's depressed mood includes pervasive hopelessness not specifically tied to the bereavement.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling hopeless?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about hopelessness, but the provided symptom profiles do not include a distinct hopelessness item. It is related to depression but not directly covered by the listed symptoms.

patient.answer:
Hopeless… I’m not completely sure how to answer that.

I don’t think I walk around thinking, “There is no hope,” in a clear way like that. It’s more that sometimes everything feels very heavy and hard to imagine changing. But I don’t know if that’s hopelessness exactly, or just being worn down and sad and stuck in the same thoughts.

There are moments when I can still picture things being a little easier someday, or at least I tell myself they might be. So I wouldn’t say I feel hopeless all the time. It’s just… I don’t feel very confident right now either, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the low mood is still tied to reminders or thoughts of the sister versus occurring independently, to distinguish adjustment disorder from a major depressive episode.
doctor.question: When you feel low, does it usually come on after something reminds you of your sister?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether low mood is triggered by reminders of her sister, which is about the pattern or trigger of sadness/grief rather than any specific symptom profile item provided.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure it’s that neat, honestly. Sometimes, yes, I’ll notice I’m thinking about her and then my mood sinks, but other times I’m already low and then I realize I’ve been sort of circling around thoughts of her in the background.

It isn’t always a clear trigger, like seeing a photograph or hearing a song or something. I wish it were that simple, because then I could at least point to it and say, “That’s what set me off.” A lot of the time it feels more gradual than that, like the sadness is just there and then attaches itself to whatever reminds me of her.

So… I guess I haven’t noticed a reliable pattern. It can be connected, but I don’t know that it usually comes on only after a reminder.

opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a roughly 1-month episode beginning after her sister’s sudden death, with depressive symptoms present nearly every day: depressed mood, markedly reduced pleasure, insomnia with early-morning awakening, recurrent passive death wishes, and guilt/self-blame. Although bereavement is the precipitant, the syndrome is not limited to momentary grief reactions and includes pervasive low mood and anhedonia even outside explicit thoughts of the sister, supporting a depressive episode over adjustment disorder.
